blocks.text: Let code look up the services it needs from a central registry, instead of receiving them.

A **locator** maps a type or name to a service instance. A class calls `Locator.get(Mailer.class)` when it needs one. This decouples the class from the concrete implementation, but dependencies become **invisible**: nothing in the constructor says what the class needs, and a missing registration fails at runtime.

items: **Benefit:** easy to retrofit, no constructor changes.

blocks.text: Treat it as the pattern that dependency injection replaces. Prefer it only where the set of services is unknown at compile time.

walkthrough.note: A static registry keyed by type. `get` fails loudly with a message naming the missing type, and a concurrent map keeps it safe across threads.
`SignupService` has no constructor parameters, so its dependency on `Mailer` is invisible until the method runs.
Startup code registers implementations. Nothing forces this to happen before first use.
Remove the registration and the same call compiles but fails at runtime. This is the cost DI avoids by moving the failure to construction.

blocks.text: A build tool discovering compiler plugins at startup.

The tool cannot know at compile time which plugins sit on the classpath. It asks the JDK's `ServiceLoader` for every `CompilerPlugin` implementation, each declared in a descriptor inside its own jar. Adding a plugin means dropping a jar in, with no change to the host. A locator fits because discovery, not wiring, is the problem.
Payoff: extensibility without recompiling the host. Pair it with DI inside the plugin so its own collaborators stay explicit.

notes.text: dependency not visible in its API

lists.title: Use when
items: Implementations are discovered at runtime, as with plugins and drivers.
Retrofitting legacy code that you can't give constructors yet.
At a framework boundary where object creation is out of your control.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: You control construction: use [Dependency Injection](kata:dependency-injection) instead.
You need compile-time or startup-time proof that dependencies exist.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Hidden dependencies make classes hard to understand and reuse.
Global mutable registry leaks state between tests.
Failures appear at the first call, possibly in production.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Business classes that call `Locator.get` several times per method.
Injecting the locator itself everywhere, which is DI in name only.

rows.difference: The class asks for services (pull) versus being handed them (push). Push makes dependencies explicit; pull hides them and fails later.
Both give global access. A singleton is one class controlling its own instance; a locator is a registry of many services replaceable by type.
A factory creates a new object on request. A locator returns an already registered one, often shared.
A locator decouples from concrete classes, as DIP asks, but still couples every client to the locator and hides what it uses.

exercises.scenario: A host application must load optional export formats from jars dropped into a folder by third parties. The host can't know the implementations at compile time and must find them at startup.

Constructor wiring needs the implementations known to the composition root, which is exactly what isn't available.
A factory method needs a subclass per format known in advance.
A global instance doesn't discover anything; it only restricts instance count.

exercises.explanation: A service must exist before it is registered, and registration must precede the first lookup. Clearing comes last, so earlier calls still find it.

exercises.prompt: Explain the Service Locator pattern and why most teams prefer dependency injection.

modelAnswer.text: A service locator is a registry that code queries for the services it needs. It decouples callers from concrete classes, but the dependencies are hidden in method bodies, global state complicates tests, and a missing registration fails at runtime. Dependency injection makes them explicit parameters. Locators remain valid for runtime plugin discovery.

keyPoints: Dependencies are hidden from the API
Valid for plugin discovery such as ServiceLoader
